adults.title: Past the Cold Oatmeal: Trusting the Lord’s Promises
adults.big_idea: When we remember the great things the Lord has already done, we can see past today’s frustrations, trust His promises, and find peace and joy in Jesus Christ now.
adults.objective: Learners will name specific times the Lord has helped them and choose one promise of His to rely on this week, feeling that it applies to them personally.
prepare: Read Elder Renlund’s talk, especially the story of Mr. Martin and the story of his sister, Linda.
Study Numbers 14:2, 11; Moroni 10:3; 2 Nephi 2:3; and John 16:33.
Bring a slip of paper and a pencil with an eraser for each person.
Write on the board: Where have I been? What has God promised?

segments.name: The breakfast tray
steps: After the opening prayer, retell the story of Mr. Martin in your own words. In the late 1980s he was dying of heart failure. His first transplanted heart did not work well. A second donor heart, one considered marginal, functioned beautifully. Ten days later, the day before going home, he sat gripping his breakfast tray, irritated that the oatmeal was not hot and the milk was not cold.
Point out that Elder Renlund tells this with affection and humor, not scorn. He says we can easily fall into the same trap.
Read the first key quote aloud. Invite everyone to think silently of one piece of “cold oatmeal” in front of them this week. No one needs to share it.
questions: Why do small, present frustrations so easily crowd out large, past mercies?

segments.name: How long will it be?
steps: Explain that Elder Renlund sees this same pattern in the children of Israel, whom the Lord had led out of Egypt, saved at the Red Sea, and fed in the wilderness.
In pairs, read Numbers 14:2 and then Numbers 14:11. Ask one partner to listen for what Israel was feeling and the other for what the Lord was asking.
Share Elder Renlund’s restatement of the Lord’s question: “Why don’t they trust me? Despite all I have done, why won’t they believe me?”
Discuss the questions as a class. Welcome honest answers; Elder Renlund acknowledges that some have been served more than their share of cold oatmeal.
questions: What do you hear in the Lord’s question: anger, sorrow, longing, something else?
Elder Renlund says Israel’s trust eroded as they overlooked both the Lord’s blessings and His promises. How does forgetting the past weaken trust in the future?

segments.name: Remember the great things
steps: Read Moroni 10:3 together and point to the two questions on the board. Then read the second key quote.
Hand out the slips of paper. Give three quiet minutes for each person to list times the Lord has inclined His ear to them: a prayer answered, strength given, a rescue seen only later.
Invite learners to turn to a neighbor and share one item from the list, as they feel comfortable.
Ask two or three people to tell the class what happened inside them as they wrote.
questions: How does looking back at what the Lord has done change the way today’s cold oatmeal looks?

segments.name: Erase the asterisk
steps: Tell the story of Elder Renlund’s sister, Linda. She read the Lord’s promises but saw in her mind a big asterisk that excepted her. Over the years she came to realize, in her words, “The blessings are promised to me too.”
Read 2 Nephi 2:3 and ask whose righteousness Lehi says Jacob’s redemption rests on. Read the key quote that begins with faith in Jesus Christ freeing us from uncertainty.
Read the Prophet Joseph Smith’s statement in the aligned quotes. Elder Renlund explains that ample provision means every human circumstance is within the Savior’s redemptive reach.

Invite each person to draw a small asterisk in pencil on the back of the slip and silently name a promise they struggle to believe is for them. Read the key quote about the asterisk, then invite them to erase it.
questions: Why is it sometimes easier to believe God’s promises for others than for ourselves?
How does it change things to rest our hope on the Savior’s faithfulness rather than on our own?

segments.name: Peace in the here and now
steps: Read John 16:33 aloud. Note that the Savior promises peace in Him while plainly saying we will have tribulation.
Share Elder Renlund’s teaching that Jesus overcame the world, so we do not have to do so ourselves. Then read President Oaks’s words from the aligned quotes.
As a check for understanding, ask one or two people to finish this sentence in their own words: I can have joy now, even with cold oatmeal, because…

segments.name: Choose and act
steps: Invite each person to write one promise of the Lord on the slip, beneath the list of times He has helped, and to choose one item from the act list.

Connect the action to what Elder Renlund taught: as we reflect on what the Lord has done, we are better positioned to grasp the bigger picture and rely on His promises, and when our faith is centered on Jesus Christ, He promises spiritual peace no matter our circumstances.
Bear a brief testimony that the Lord keeps His promises. If time allows, sing or read the chorus of “Standing on the Promises,” which Elder Renlund quoted.
Next week, begin by asking: When did remembering change how a hard moment looked?

key_quotes.text: We focus on the here and now—the “cold oatmeal”—and lose sight of the bigger picture, both where we have been and God’s promises to us.

As we reflect on the great things the Lord has already done and remember His goodness and mercy, we are better positioned to grasp the bigger picture and to rely on His promises to us. We can trust Him.
Faith in Jesus Christ frees us from uncertainty because our hope rests on His faithfulness and righteousness, not on our own.
there is no asterisk excluding you from God’s richest blessings. If you think there is, take out a big eraser and obliterate that asterisk. You can rely on God’s promises.

scriptures.use: Read in pairs. One partner listens for what Israel felt, the other for what the Lord asked. Then discuss what erodes trust.
Read together before the silent writing. Use it to frame the list of times the Lord has been merciful to each learner.
Read aloud and ask whose righteousness Jacob’s redemption rests on. Connect it to erasing the asterisk.
Read near the end. Notice that peace in Christ and tribulation in the world are promised in the same verse.

aligned_quotes.speaker: The Prophet Joseph Smith
aligned_quotes.text: knows the situation of both the living and the dead, and has made ample provision for their redemption, according to their several circumstances, and the laws of the kingdom of God, whether in this world, or in the world to come.

aligned_quotes.speaker: President Oaks
aligned_quotes.text: These promises from the Book of Mormon are true. Millions believe them and have had experiences to affirm their truth. I invite all to believe them.

takeaways: Cold oatmeal is real, but it is not the whole picture.
Remembering what the Lord has done helps me trust what He has promised.
There is no asterisk excluding me from God’s promises.
act: Keep your slip where you will see it each morning and add one more time the Lord has helped you every day this week.
When a frustration looms, stop and ask the two questions: Where have I been? What has God promised?
Choose one scriptural promise you have privately marked with an asterisk. Pray about it by name and tell Heavenly Father you want to trust Him.
Tell a family member or friend about one great thing the Lord has done for you.
adapt: At home: do the remembering list aloud around the table, taking turns until everyone has named three times the Lord has helped.
Large class: do the sharing in threes rather than as a whole class so that everyone speaks.
Short on time: keep the breakfast tray, the remembering list, and the asterisk; summarize Numbers 14 in a sentence.

youth.title: Zoom Out: No Asterisk Next to Your Name
youth.big_idea: When we zoom out and remember what the Lord has already done, we can trust that His promises are for us, with no exceptions, and find peace in Him even on hard days.
youth.objective: Youth will list specific things the Lord has done for them and identify one promise of God they will choose to believe applies to them.
prepare: Read Elder Renlund’s talk. Be ready to tell the stories of Mr. Martin and of Linda in your own words.
Bring an index card or half sheet and a pencil with an eraser for each person.
Write three references on the board: Exodus 14:11–12, Exodus 16:2–4, Exodus 17:3–6.
Ask the youth to have their phones or scriptures ready.

segments.name: Zoom in, zoom out
steps: As soon as the prayer ends, ask everyone to open a photo on their phone and zoom in as far as it will go. If phones are not available, hold a paper tube up to a picture in the room.
Have each person show the zoomed-in screen to a neighbor, who gets three guesses at what it is. Then zoom out.
Say: Today is about what happens when we live zoomed in.
questions: What could you not tell about the picture until you zoomed out?

segments.name: The oatmeal isn’t hot
steps: Tell the story of Mr. Martin. In the late 1980s he was dying of heart failure. His first heart transplant did not work well. A second donor heart, one no one else would use, functioned beautifully. Ten days later, about to go home, he was gripping his breakfast tray, irritated that the oatmeal was not hot and the milk was not cold.
Read the first key quote. Explain that Elder Renlund calls our zoomed-in frustrations “cold oatmeal.”
Ask each person to tell a neighbor one harmless piece of cold oatmeal from this week: a slow connection, a bad grade, a chore.
questions: Why is it so easy to forget something huge and good when something small and annoying is right in front of us?

segments.name: Evidence hunt
steps: Divide into three teams and assign each team one reference from the board.

Give four minutes. Each team finds two things: what Israel complained about, and, by reading the verses just before and after, what the Lord had done or was about to do for them. The team with the clearest two-column list wins.
Have each team report in thirty seconds.

Explain that when Israel reached the promised land they were intimidated and complained again. Read Numbers 14:11 aloud, then Elder Renlund’s restatement: “Why don’t they trust me? Despite all I have done, why won’t they believe me?”
questions: If you had walked through the Red Sea, do you think you would still have complained? Why do people forget?
What do you think the Lord was feeling when He asked that question?

segments.name: The asterisk
steps: Tell Linda’s story. Elder Renlund’s younger sister read the Lord’s promises in the scriptures but saw a big asterisk in her mind, as if the blessings applied to everyone except her. Later she realized, “The blessings are promised to me too.”

Hand out cards and pencils. Ask each person to draw an asterisk and, privately, think of a promise of God that feels like it is for other people: being forgiven, being heard, feeling peace. No one will see the cards.

Read 2 Nephi 2:3 together and ask whose righteousness Jacob’s redemption depended on. Read the key quote about hope resting on the Savior’s faithfulness, and share President Oaks’s words from the aligned quotes.
Read the key quote about the asterisk. Invite everyone to erase theirs.
Be honest about the hard question below. Read John 16:33 and note that the Savior promises peace in Him, not a life without tribulation. Share Elder Dunn’s words from the aligned quotes.
questions: Why might someone your age feel like the exception to God’s promises?
What about when I have prayed and the hard thing has not changed? What does John 16:33 actually promise?

segments.name: Zoom-out list
steps: Read the second key quote, which begins with striving to remember.
Give three minutes: in a phone note or on the back of the card, each person lists at least five things the Lord has done for them. Title it “Great things.”
Invite a few volunteers to share one item. Share one of your own.
As a check for understanding, ask one person to explain to the class, in one sentence, what cold oatmeal means and what the cure is.
questions: How do you feel about your cold oatmeal after writing that list?

segments.name: Challenge for the week
steps: Offer the challenge: add one line to your list every day for seven days, and when cold oatmeal shows up, open the list before you complain.

Explain why it is worth doing. Elder Renlund taught that as we remember the Lord’s goodness and mercy we are better positioned to grasp the bigger picture and rely on His promises, and that the Savior promises spiritual peace no matter our circumstances when our faith is centered on Him.
Bear your testimony that God’s promises are for each person in the room. Sing or read the chorus of “Standing on the Promises” if you wish.
Next week, start class by asking who kept the list for seven days and what they noticed.

key_quotes.text: We focus on the here and now—the “cold oatmeal”—and lose sight of the bigger picture, both where we have been and God’s promises to us.
Strive to remember all the times He has inclined His ear to you, especially when confronted with cold oatmeal.
Faith in Jesus Christ frees us from uncertainty because our hope rests on His faithfulness and righteousness, not on our own.
there is no asterisk excluding you from God’s richest blessings. If you think there is, take out a big eraser and obliterate that asterisk. You can rely on God’s promises.

scriptures.use: One of three team passages (with Exodus 14:11–12 and 17:3–6). Teams list what Israel complained about and what the Lord did for them.
Read aloud after the teams report. Ask what the Lord was feeling when He asked this question.
Read together during the asterisk activity. Ask whose righteousness Jacob’s redemption depended on.
Read when discussing prayers that seem unanswered. Notice what the Savior does and does not promise.

aligned_quotes.speaker: Elder Dunn
aligned_quotes.text: Peace will come even when hoped-for outcomes do not.

takeaways: Zoomed in, I see cold oatmeal; zoomed out, I see what the Lord has done.
My hope rests on the Savior’s righteousness, not on my being good enough.
God’s promises have no asterisk next to my name.
act: Add one line a day for seven days to your list of great things the Lord has done for you.
Before you complain about something this week, read your list first.
Find one promise in the scriptures, put your own name in it, and pray about it.
Tell a friend or family member who is having a rough week one thing the Lord has done for you.
adapt: At home: do the zoom game with a family photo, then make one shared family list of great things the Lord has done.
Very small class: skip the teams and read Exodus 16:2–4 together, building the two-column list on the board.
Short on time: keep the zoom game, Linda’s story with the eraser, and the list.

children.title: Jesus Keeps His Promises
children.big_idea: Heavenly Father and Jesus have done great things for me, and They always keep Their promises.
children.objective: Children will name good things Heavenly Father and Jesus have done for them and say that Jesus keeps His promises to them.
prepare: Read the first five paragraphs of Elder Renlund’s talk and his story about his sister, Linda.
Bring a large picture (a Gospel Art picture of the Savior works well) and a sheet of paper rolled into a tube.
Bring a blanket or sheet, a soft ball, paper, crayons, and a pencil with an eraser for each child.
Write on the board: Jesus keeps His promises.

segments.name: Peek through the tube
steps: Greet each child by name and invite a child to pray.
Hold the picture facing you. Let each child look through the paper tube at one small corner of it and guess what the picture is.
Turn the picture around so everyone sees all of it. Say: When we look at only one little part, we miss the big picture.
Teach the truth on the board with actions: point up for Jesus, cross your arms like a hug for keeps, and stamp both feet for promises. Say it together three times.
questions: What could you see when you looked at the whole picture?

segments.name: The grumpy breakfast
steps: Tell the story simply. Elder Renlund was a doctor. A man named Mr. Martin was very sick because his heart did not work well. He was given a new heart, and it worked beautifully. He was getting better and could soon go home. That was a great blessing.
Then one morning Mr. Martin was grumpy. Invite the children to show a grumpy face. He said his oatmeal was not hot and his milk was not cold.
Explain that Mr. Martin was looking at one little thing, like looking through the tube. He forgot the great big blessing.
Say the truth together again with the actions.
questions: What big blessing did Mr. Martin forget?
What helps you feel better when you are grumpy?

segments.name: Through the Red Sea
steps: Tell the children that long ago Heavenly Father led His people, the children of Israel, out of Egypt, where they had been slaves.

Have two helpers hold the blanket low like water. The people came to the Red Sea and could not get across. The Lord made a path through the sea. Lift the blanket high and let the children walk under it to the other side.
On the other side, say: The people were hungry and thirsty, and the Lord gave them food and water. Have the children pretend to gather food from the ground.
Say: Even after all that, the people sometimes grumbled and forgot. Show a grumpy face, then a remembering face. Walk back under the blanket saying: The Lord helped us.
Tell them the Lord said, “I will never break my covenant with you.” A covenant is a sacred promise. Say the truth with actions.
questions: What great things did the Lord do for His people?

segments.name: Remember ball
steps: Sit in a circle. Explain that Elder Renlund taught us to remember the good things the Lord has done.

Roll the ball to a child. That child names one good thing Heavenly Father or Jesus has given or done for them, then rolls the ball to someone else. Offer ideas if a child is unsure: the sun, my body, the scriptures, prayer.
After each answer, everyone says together: Thank you, Heavenly Father.
Go around until every child has had at least one turn.

segments.name: Erase the star
steps: Give each child paper and a pencil. Tell them Elder Renlund’s sister, Linda, once thought God’s blessings were for everyone except her. It was as if she saw a little star mark that meant not you. Then she learned that the blessings were promised to her too.
Have each child draw a small star in pencil in the corner of the paper. Say together: God’s promises are for me. Then let them erase the star.
Hand out crayons. Invite each child to draw one good thing Heavenly Father or Jesus has done for them.
As they draw, go to each child, ask about the picture, and say: Jesus keeps His promises to you.

segments.name: Sing and share
steps: Sing “My Heavenly Father Loves Me” or the chorus of “Count Your Blessings.”
As a check, ask the children to finish your sentence: Jesus keeps His… Then let two or three children hold up their drawings and tell about them.
Invite the children to tell Heavenly Father one thing they are thankful for in their prayer each night this week, and to take their drawing home to show someone.

Read Elder Fale’s words from the aligned quotes and have the children repeat them. Bear a short testimony that Heavenly Father and Jesus always keep Their promises. Next week, begin by asking what they thanked Heavenly Father for.

key_quotes.text: I will never break my covenant with you.
We can trust the Lord, especially His promises. These promises apply to you.
You can rely on God’s promises.

scriptures.use: Tell this story in your own words while the children walk under the blanket. An older child may read verse 22 aloud.
Share the Lord’s promise from this verse, as Elder Renlund quoted it, after the Red Sea activity. Explain that a covenant is a sacred promise.
For older children: read it aloud and ask what Moroni wants us to remember. Use it to introduce the remember ball.

aligned_quotes.speaker: Elder Fale
aligned_quotes.text: I am a child of God and He loves me.

takeaways: Heavenly Father and Jesus have done great things for me.
I can remember my blessings and say thank you.
Jesus keeps His promises to me.
act: Tell Heavenly Father one thing you are thankful for in your prayer each night.
When you feel grumpy, stop and name one good thing Heavenly Father has given you.
Show your drawing to someone at home and tell them that Jesus keeps His promises.

adapt.younger: For ages 3–7: keep the stories to three or four sentences each and repeat the truth with actions after every activity. Let helpers hold the blanket and go under it twice. Draw the star for children who need help and let them do the erasing. In the remember ball, accept any answer and offer a choice of two if a child is shy.
adapt.older: For ages 8–11: have a child read Exodus 14:22 and another read Moroni 10:3 aloud. Let an older child lead the remember ball. Ask a harder question: Why do you think the people forgot the Red Sea so quickly, and what helps you remember? Invite them to write three blessings beside their drawing.
